object_types.name: Vendor
object_types.definition: A supplier from which the business procures goods, services, or materials. Vendors are onboarded and tracked for procurement and compliance purposes.

source_references.excerpt: The vendor record. It's the thing in the supplier master... Vendor number. Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.
It's the thing we quote in every conversation with AP... It's the primary key. It's been the primary key since before I got here.

object_types.name: VendorNumber
object_types.definition: The unique system-generated identifier assigned to each vendor upon record creation.

source_references.excerpt: Vendor number. Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created... It's the thing we quote in every conversation with AP.

object_types.name: LegalName
object_types.definition: The official registered legal name of the vendor entity.

source_references.excerpt: Legal name. Tax ID. Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

object_types.name: TaxId
object_types.definition: The tax identification number for the vendor (e.g., W-9 for US vendors). Not unique in the system due to duplicate onboarding and parent-subsidiary structures.

source_references.excerpt: Tax ID... We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them.

object_types.name: VendorAddress
object_types.definition: The vendor's address. The system tracks three types: legal address, remit-to address (for invoicing), and ship-from address (for goods shipment).

source_references.excerpt: Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

object_types.name: VendorStatus
object_types.definition: The operational status of the vendor record. Allowed values are draft, active, or suspended.

source_references.excerpt: Draft, active, suspended... It defaults to draft the moment the record is created.

object_types.name: SpendTier
object_types.definition: The procurement spend category assigned to the vendor, based on annual spend volume and strategic importance. Bronze (default, lowest spend), Silver (medium spend), or Gold (highest spend, strategic vendor).

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a tier. Bronze, silver, gold... Gold vendors are the ones we spend real money with, they get quarterly business reviews, better payment terms, a named relationship manager.
Every vendor gets a spend tier. Bronze by default if nobody's assessed them.

object_types.name: RiskTier
object_types.definition: The compliance risk category assigned to the vendor based on the risk review, reflecting data sensitivity, geography, and sole-source dependency. Low, medium, or high risk.

source_references.excerpt: I use low, medium, high... based on the review -- what data they touch, what geography they operate in, whether they're a sole source.
Risk tier comes from the review, so a vendor without a review has no risk tier... It's set by the review. A vendor with no review has no risk tier.

object_types.name: RiskReview
object_types.definition: A compliance assessment of a vendor recording risk factors, approvals, and sign-offs. Each review is a historical record that accumulates over the vendor's lifecycle. A vendor must have a current signed-off review to be in active status.

source_references.excerpt: Every active vendor has exactly one completed risk review... A vendor accumulates review records over time. At most one is the current one. Being active requires a current signed-off review.
The review is its own record. It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.

object_types.name: ReviewId
object_types.definition: The unique system-generated identifier for a risk review record.

source_references.excerpt: It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.

object_types.name: Region
object_types.definition: A geographic operational region served by vendors. Each region is identified by a fixed code (EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM). Used to manage regional vendor contacts since a vendor may operate in multiple regions with different account teams.

source_references.excerpt: Since we went to regional sourcing last year, it's one primary contact per region... A given vendor in a given region has exactly one primary contact.
Region code. EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM.

object_types.name: RegionCode
object_types.definition: The code that uniquely identifies a geographic region.

source_references.excerpt: Region code. EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM.

object_types.name: Contact
object_types.definition: A primary contact person for a vendor within a specific region. Each vendor-region combination has at most one primary contact. Contains the contact's name, email, and phone number.

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact. Name, email, phone number... A given vendor in a given region has exactly one primary contact.

ambiguities.description: Address modeling: The transcript indicates vendors have three address types (legal, remit-to, ship-from) that are frequently different and often wrong. The current model treats 'VendorAddress' as a single value type. It is unclear whether the system stores all three addresses as separate values (requiring three binary facts: 'Vendor has LegalAddress', 'Vendor has RemitToAddress', 'Vendor has ShipFromAddress'), a single composite address, or a single address with address type metadata. This affects whether addresses should be modeled as three distinct facts or remain as a single fact with richer structure.

source_references.excerpt: Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

ambiguities.description: Risk tier optional participation: The model specifies that risk tier is optional for draft vendors (a draft vendor has no risk tier) but mandatory for active vendors (active vendors have a current signed-off review and thus a risk tier). However, the constraint 'Vendor has RiskTier' lacks a mandatory constraint, making it appear the relationship is always optional. The business rule should be: active vendors must have a risk tier; draft vendors may not have one. This requires either (a) a disjunctive constraint combining vendor status and risk tier, or (b) marking risk tier as mandatory on active vendors only (conditional mandatory), which the current model does not formally support.

source_references.excerpt: Risk tier comes from the review, so a vendor without a review has no risk tier... Every _active_ vendor has a current signed-off review. A draft vendor has no review at all -- that's the normal case, that's what draft means.

ambiguities.description: Current review identification: The transcript states that a vendor can have multiple risk reviews over its lifecycle, but at most one is 'current.' The model includes a RiskReview entity and a mandatory 'RiskReview belongs to Vendor' relationship for active vendors. However, there is no explicit way to mark which review is current. Either (a) RiskReview needs an attribute like 'IsCurrent' (boolean), or (b) the relationship 'Vendor has RiskTier' should reference the current review by its ID or via a derived relationship. Without this, the model cannot express why an active vendor with multiple reviews uses one over the others.

source_references.excerpt: A vendor can have several reviews over its life -- we re-review on a cycle, and every re-review is a new record, we don't edit the old one... A vendor accumulates review records over time. At most one is the current one.

ambiguities.description: Risk review sign-off tracking: The transcript repeatedly emphasizes that a review must be 'signed off' to activate a vendor, but the model includes no explicit attribute to track the sign-off status or auditor identity. Raj states, 'Every active vendor has exactly one completed risk review' and 'the one has to be signed off.' The review is tracked for audit purposes to know 'who signed it and when.' The model should include an attribute like 'ReviewSignOffDate' and possibly 'SignedByPerson' to capture this critical compliance fact.

source_references.excerpt: Every active vendor has exactly one completed risk review... A review has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.

ambiguities.description: Spend tier vs. risk tier terminology conflict: The transcript identifies a critical naming conflict: both procurement and compliance use the term 'tier,' but procurement means 'spend tier' (gold, silver, bronze) and compliance means 'risk tier' (low, medium, high). These are modeled as separate facts and fields. However, end users do not consistently disambiguate. The phrase 'high tier vendor' in meetings is genuinely ambiguous (big spender vs. dangerous). The model assumes this is a documentation/training issue, not a data issue, and does not attempt to enforce naming. This ambiguity could lead to communication errors if stakeholders refer to one tier by the generic term.

source_references.excerpt: You both call it 'tier'... Someone says 'that's a high tier vendor' in a meeting and half the room hears 'big spender' and the other half hears 'dangerous,' and those are very different conversations... Most of our cloud providers are exactly that. Big spend, high risk.

ambiguities.description: Vendor contact regional scope and optionality: The model requires that if a vendor operates in a region, it must have a primary contact for that region (via the ternary 'Vendor operates in Region with Contact'). However, the transcript does not explicitly state whether every region a vendor operates in must have a contact assigned, or whether a vendor can operate in a region without a contact. The statement 'If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all' suggests a vendor may simply not be present in all regions, but does not clarify whether a newly added region requires immediate contact assignment.

source_references.excerpt: Can a vendor have no contact in a region?... If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all. Most of our vendors are one region only.

ambiguities.description: In-flight purchase order handling on vendor suspension: The transcript explicitly flags an unresolved policy question: what should happen to purchase orders already in flight when a vendor is suspended? Raj's position is that suspension should halt all POs immediately (for compliance). Dana's position is that this is operationally impossible (goods already shipped). Mei notes that in practice, people suspend the vendor and quietly allow open POs to run (undocumented). The facilitator parks this as out of scope, noting that the current model captures only the creation-time control (active vendors only) and nothing about post-suspension behavior. No constraint is modeled for this scenario because there is no agreed rule yet.

source_references.excerpt: You can't raise one against a vendor who isn't active... Parking it explicitly: what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended is undecided. Today's model captures three statuses and the creation-time control, and nothing about post-suspension fulfilment, because there is nothing agreed to capture.

ambiguities.description: Draft vendor status constraints: The transcript states that vendors default to draft status when created and that draft vendors have no risk tier (because they have no review yet). However, the model does not explicitly constrain when a vendor can transition from draft to active, what triggers the transition, or what happens if a vendor is in draft for an extended period. The only stated rule is that 'you cannot move a vendor to active without a completed [signed-off] review.' This models the gate, but not the process or timeline.

source_references.excerpt: It defaults to draft the moment the record is created... A draft vendor has no review at all -- that's the normal case, that's what draft means.

ambiguities.description: Preferred vendor flagging: Mei maintains a spreadsheet with a 'preferred' flag indicating which vendor to buy from when multiple vendors can supply the same thing. This flag is recognized informally across procurement but is not in the system and has no formal process. The facilitator explicitly notes this as a gap rather than a rule, because the criteria are ad hoc (decided by Mei and 'whoever's shouting loudest that week'). The model does not include this relationship because there is no defined, consistent rule to model.

source_references.excerpt: There's a column called 'preferred.' It means if two vendors can supply the same thing, buy from this one... Officially nobody. In practice, me and whoever's shouting loudest that week... Don't model it.

ambiguities.description: Vendor duplicate records: The transcript notes that duplicate vendor records exist (same company onboarded twice, same tax ID for multiple legal entities under a parent). A cleanup project has been on the roadmap for two years but is out of scope for this model. Tax ID is explicitly not a reliable identifier. The model captures vendor_number as the sole identifier but does not address the data quality issue or model any relationship between duplicate records.

source_references.excerpt: We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them... The duplicates are also a compliance problem, for what it's worth. If we've got the same entity twice we can't see aggregate exposure.

ambiguities.description: System enforcement of business rules: The transcript reveals that some rules are system-enforced (e.g., you cannot transition a vendor to active without a completed review; a PO form requires a vendor to be selected) and others are manual/procedural (e.g., assigning spend tier, flagging preferred vendors). The model does not distinguish between system constraints and process constraints. This is not necessarily an error but may be important for implementation and audit purposes.

source_references.excerpt: The system does enforce it -- you cannot move a vendor to active without a completed review, the transition is blocked... You can't create one without picking a vendor. The form won't let you.
